Doleful
DOHL-ful
adjective
From the Old French doel, grief, and that from the Latin dolere, to grieve or suffer pain — the root of dolour and condole. Full of grief; expressing or causing sorrow.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Doleful appears twice, and both instances are sounds of desolation. In the oracle against Babylon, “their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there” (Isa 13:21) — the Hebrew is literally howling things, creatures whose cry is a wail, filling the rooms where a court once sat. And in Micah, the sound comes from the people themselves: “In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people” (Mic 2:4). The Hebrew here is a striking construction, a wailing of wailings, grief piled upon its own word. What is being mourned is instructive — he hath changed the portion of my people. Micah had been indicting men who coveted fields and took them, who oppressed a man and his house, and the judgment answers the sin exactly: those who moved the boundaries of other men’s portions find their own portion changed and divided among strangers. Scripture does not treat such lament as unbelief. It records it, gives it words, and sets whole books in its key. But it also refuses to leave the reader there: the same prophet who writes the wailing of wailings ends his book asking Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?

Webster 1828 Definition

Full of grief; sorrowful; expressing or causing dolour. Used of the howling creatures of a ruined city and of a lamentation piled upon itself.

DOLEFUL, adj. Sorrowful; expressing grief; as a doleful whine.

Melancholy; afflicted; full of grief.

Dismal; impressing sorrow; gloomy; as a doleful place.

From the Old French doel, grief; Latin dolere, to grieve; whence dolour.

Isa 13:21: doleful creatures, in the Hebrew literally howling things.

Key Scripture

Isa 13:21 — "But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there."

Mic 2:4 — "In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields."

Mic 2:2 — "And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage."

Mic 7:18 — "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy."

Modern Corruption

Lament has been squeezed out of ordinary church life by an expectation of relentless positivity, leaving grieving believers without permitted language — though Scripture supplies whole books of it.

expand to see more

The corruption is the demand for perpetual brightness. A great deal of modern religious culture has no settled place for sorrow that does not resolve quickly: songs are chosen for their lift, testimonies for their happy ending, and the believer in prolonged grief learns to answer fine because the alternative unsettles the room. Scripture is far broader. Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament, an entire book is named Lamentations, Job sits in ashes for chapters, and the prophets wail. Micah’s doleful lamentation is a wailing of wailings — grief doubled in the grammar itself. God gave His people this vocabulary; a church that will not use it has silenced part of inspired speech.

Recover the plain sense: lament is not the opposite of faith but one of its languages, and it is addressed to God rather than merely about circumstances. Note also what Micah mourns: he hath changed the portion of my people, a judgment fitted precisely to the sin of Mic 2:2, where men coveted fields and took them by violence. The lament is honest about deserving. That is what distinguishes biblical grief from mere despair — it tells the truth about God’s justice while it weeps. And it does not end there. The prophet who wrote the wailing of wailings closes his book with Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin dolere, to grieve — full of sorrow; the howling of a ruined city and the wailing of wailings.

expand to see more

Doleful — Old French doel, grief; Latin dolere, to suffer pain.

Kin to dolour, condole, and indolent (literally, feeling no pain).

Isa 13:21: the Hebrew for doleful creatures is literally howling things.

Mic 2:4: a doleful lamentation is in Hebrew a wailing of wailings.

The judgment answers the sin: those who moved others’ portions lose their own.
